scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Ballet de cour developed in late 16th-century France out of medieval processions, mummeries, and Italian Renaissance court festivals.
Catherine de' Medici championed these entertainments following her 1533 marriage to Henri II, bringing Italian staging concepts to Paris.
The Académie de Poésie et de Musique, established in 1570 by Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville, provided the philosophical ambition to harmonize dance, verse, and music.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ballets de cour marked royal weddings, state receptions of foreign ambassadors, and celebrations of political triumphs.

As a secular ceremony designed to exalt the State and project royal power, it communicated harmony, virtue, and monarchical dominance, often using classical allegory to symbolize national reconciliation after religious civil strife.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Spectacles were staged in large palace halls, such as the Tuileries Palace and the Louvre, before the advent of the proscenium stage.
Decor was lavish, featuring elaborate scenic machinery such as chariot-floats, palaces, gardens, townscapes, and three-tiered fountains.
Costumes were ornate aristocratic dress, later evolving toward lighter apparel and flexible footwear by the late 17th century.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historic figures include Queen Catherine de' Medici; choreographer and master of revels Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx (Baldassarino de Belgioioso); poet Isaac de Benserade; Académie founders Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville; monarchs Henri III, Louis XIII, and Louis XIV; composer Jean-Baptiste Lully; and ballet superintendent Pierre Beauchamp.

Originating in the French royal court in Paris and its royal residences (such as the Tuileries, the Louvre, and Chantilly), the form rapidly spread to courts across Europe, contrasting with Italian opera which concentrated more heavily on singing than physical choreography.

Evolved from medieval mummeries and Italian Renaissance court festivals into French court ballet; later transformed into comédie-ballet and opéra-ballet, directly providing the technical and organizational foundation for codified classical ballet.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Ballet de cour is child of comédie-ballet: Developed directly out of the ballet de cour under Lully and Molière after 1670.
Ballet de cour is child of opéra-ballet: Emerged as a full theatrical successor driven by Lully when court ballets lost royal performance.
Ballet de cour is child of classical ballet: Derived its five codified positions and structural discipline from Beauchamp's work in court ballets.

Representation of a Ballet before Henri III. and his Court, in the Gallery of the Louvre. Re-engraving from an original on Copper in theBallet comique de la Royne by Balthazar de Beaujoyeulx (Paris: Ballard,1582).
According to T.E. Lawrenson, The French Stage and Playhouse in the Seventeenth Century (2nd ed., 1986), p. 184, this performance took place in the Petit Bourbon.

images.description: Woodcut of a court ballet performed at the Tuileries Palace, Paris, in 1573 in honour of Polish envoys visiting to present the throne of Poland to Catherine de' Medici's son Henry, Duke of Anjou, the future Henry III of France. Sixteen court ladies, each representing a province of France, are here arranged in a figure. Among the dancers was Marguerite de Valois, Catherine's daughter.
